value.overview: The Southern Beardless-Tyrannulet is a small, active tyrant flycatcher of the American tropics. It occupies a broad range from Costa Rica and Panama south through much of South America, including Trinidad. Unlike many forest-dependent flycatchers, it often uses scrub, woodland edges, second growth, gallery forest, plantations, parks, and gardens. Its restless movements, raised crest, distinctive calls, and habit of searching foliage for insects make it easier to detect than its subdued plumage might suggest.
value.classification: The Southern Beardless-Tyrannulet belongs to the tyrant flycatcher family, Tyrannidae, and the subfamily Elaeniinae. It is one of two closely related species in the genus Camptostoma; the other is the Northern Beardless-Tyrannulet, Camptostoma imberbe.
value.identification: This small tyrannulet is about 10–11 cm long, with olive-gray to gray-brown upperparts and paler underparts. The throat and breast are whitish or pale gray, while the belly is often washed yellow, especially in some populations. Two pale wing-bars, pale feather edging, a dark eye line, and a short, broad bill are useful field marks. The crown can look slightly peaked, particularly when the bird is excited or calling. Sexes are generally alike.
value.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from Costa Rica and Panama across most of northern, western, central, and eastern South America, reaching Argentina, Uruguay, and southern Brazil. In Costa Rica it is a resident of the Pacific slope, especially southwestern areas, extending north toward the Tempisque Valley; it is not normally a widespread Caribbean-slope bird. It uses secondary forest, gallery forest, riparian thickets, dry woodland, scrub, forest edges, open country with scattered trees, plantations, parks, and gardens, generally from lowlands to about 1,200 m.
value.migrationStatus: Southern Beardless-Tyrannulets in Costa Rica are resident rather than regular long-distance migrants. Individuals may make local movements in response to food, rainfall, or habitat conditions, but the Costa Rican population remains in the country year-round. The species is also resident across most of its South American range, although some regional or elevational movements occur.
value.breeding: In Central America, breeding is generally reported during the dry-to-early-rainy-season period, with records in Costa Rica concentrated approximately from December through March, though timing can vary locally. The female builds a bulky, enclosed or globular nest with a side entrance, using plant fibers, grasses, bark, spider web, and other soft materials. Nests may be well concealed in shrubs or trees at variable heights. The usual clutch is two eggs, and both parents feed the nestlings.
value.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of insects and other small arthropods, including beetles, flies, caterpillars, spiders, and similar prey. It usually forages actively through foliage in the lower and middle levels of trees and shrubs, picking prey from leaves and twigs. It also makes short sallies to capture flying insects and may take small fruits or berries, particularly when arthropod food is less available.
value.behavior: This is a restless, conspicuous little flycatcher that often moves in pairs or small groups, sometimes joining mixed-species feeding flocks. It frequently flicks through foliage, pauses briefly on exposed twigs, and raises its crest while calling or investigating disturbances. Its calls are high, clear whistles and descending notes, and birds may respond strongly to imitations or recordings. It commonly occupies open, lightly wooded habitats and tolerates moderate human disturbance.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered stable.
